title: A Beginner's Guide to Personal Budgeting
excerpt: Learn a straightforward first-month budgeting routine using actual income, essential costs and a flexible review.
introduction: A personal budget is a plan for money you expect to receive and spend. It can start with a notebook and improve as you collect more accurate records.
author: Hisabki Kitab Editorial Team

blocks.text: New budgeters can feel they need a perfect spreadsheet or a strict rule before they begin. That can delay a simple plan that would already help.
Start with take-home income, list necessary expenses and due dates, then decide what remains for savings and flexible costs. Use your own records rather than a generic percentage rule.

Amir has a fictional PKR 50,000 monthly take-home amount. He plans PKR 32,000 for essential bills and daily needs, PKR 5,000 for a savings goal and PKR 13,000 for flexible spending and irregular costs.
50,000 - 32,000 - 5,000 = PKR 13,000. The remaining amount still needs a plan for flexible purchases and costs that do not arrive every month.

items: Write down reliable take-home income and payment dates.
List regular bills and estimate variable essentials from recent records.
Include a planned savings amount that fits your current situation.
Check that planned categories do not exceed income.
Review the plan weekly and adjust after unexpected changes.
Using gross income instead of take-home money.
Copying someone else?s category limits without checking your own costs.
Giving every rupee a plan but leaving no room for irregular expenses.

blocks.text: Use your first month to learn. Record the actual amounts and revise estimates rather than blaming yourself for a forecast that changed.
The best beginner budget is clear enough to guide a choice and easy enough to revisit next week.

faqs.question: Do I need an app to make my first budget?
faqs.answer: No. Use a method you can keep up with; an app may help organize records and review the plan.

faqs.question: What should I do if planned expenses exceed income?
faqs.answer: Check estimates and flexible costs, protect essential needs, and look at realistic changes in timing or income. Avoid assuming borrowed money solves a recurring shortfall.
